◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Partial differential equations govern almost all of continuous physics — heat flow, waves, fluids, electromagnetism, quantum mechanics. Classifying them tells you what behavior to expect and which methods apply.

PDE & classification
A PDE relates a multivariable function to its PARTIAL derivatives. Second-order linear PDEs Au_xx + Bu_xy + Cu_yy + ... classify by the discriminant B² − 4AC: <0 elliptic (Laplace, steady state), =0 parabolic (heat, diffusion), >0 hyperbolic (wave).
WORKED EXAMPLE — classifying the big three

Heat equation u_t = α u_xx: parabolic (models diffusion, smoothing over time).

Wave equation u_tt = c² u_xx: hyperbolic (models propagation at finite speed).

Laplace's equation u_xx + u_yy = 0: elliptic (models equilibrium/steady state).

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

An ODE has ONE independent variable; a PDE has two or more (e.g. space AND time). The number of variables — and the classification — dictates the solution methods.

📊 FIGURE — The three PDE families at a glance
Parabolic (heat): profiles smooth out one-way in time. Hyperbolic (wave): shapes travel and reflect, keeping energy. Elliptic (Laplace): no time at all — an equilibrium shape balancing its boundary values. Classification tells you what behavior and what data to expect.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A PDE alone has infinitely many solutions; boundary and initial conditions pin down the one that matches reality — the fixed temperature at a rod's ends, the initial shape of a plucked string.

Condition types
Initial conditions specify the state at t = 0 (needed for time-evolving heat/wave equations). Boundary conditions specify behavior at the spatial edges: DIRICHLET fixes the value (u = 0), NEUMANN fixes the derivative/flux (u_x = 0, insulated).
WORKED EXAMPLE — a heat problem setup

A rod of length L, insulated sides, ends held at 0°: BCs u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0 (Dirichlet).

Initial temperature profile: u(x,0) = f(x) (initial condition). Together these make the problem well-posed — a unique solution exists.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The heat/wave equations need BOTH initial conditions (in time) and boundary conditions (in space). Laplace's equation, having no time variable, needs only boundary conditions.

📊 FIGURE — Boundary conditions on a heated rod
The PDE governs the interior; the ends need their own rules. Dirichlet: hold the VALUE (ice bath at u = 0). Neumann: hold the FLUX (an insulated end, u_x = 0, lets nothing escape). Well-posedness = PDE + boundary conditions + initial profile.
📊 FIGURE — second order in time needs two conditions
🎯 EXAM TIP
\"Released from rest\" is the initial-velocity condition u_t(x, 0) = 0. The wave equation is second order in time, so it needs two initial conditions: the shape u(x, 0) = f(x) and the velocity. Do not confuse these with the boundary conditions u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0, which say the ends are held fixed.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

First-order PDEs (like transport/advection) are solved by the method of characteristics: the PDE reduces to ODEs along special curves where the solution stays constant — the mathematics of things being carried along by a flow.

Method of characteristics
For the transport equation u_t + c u_x = 0, the solution is constant along the characteristic lines x − ct = const. So u(x,t) = f(x − ct): the initial profile f simply travels right at speed c.
WORKED EXAMPLE — transport solution

Solve u_t + 2u_x = 0 with u(x,0) = e^{−x²}.

Characteristics: x − 2t = const, so u(x,t) = f(x − 2t) = e^{−(x−2t)²} — the initial bump moves rightward at speed 2, unchanged in shape.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

For the transport equation the profile moves WITHOUT changing shape (no diffusion). Don't confuse it with the heat equation, which smooths and spreads the profile out over time.

📊 FIGURE — Characteristics in the x–t plane
For u_t + c·u_x = 0, the lines x − ct = constant are highways: the initial value at each point rides its line unchanged. To find u(x, t), trace the characteristic through (x, t) back to t = 0 and read off the initial data there.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Separation of variables is THE classical technique: assume the solution is a product u(x,t) = X(x)T(t), and the PDE splits into ordinary differential equations — turning a hard PDE into familiar ODEs.

Separation of variables
Substitute u(x,t) = X(x)T(t). The PDE separates into X''/X = T'/(αT) = −λ (a constant). Solve the two ODEs; the boundary conditions restrict λ to discrete EIGENVALUES, giving a family of product solutions summed by superposition.
WORKED EXAMPLE — heat equation modes

For u_t = α u_xx on [0,L] with u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0, separation gives X'' + λX = 0 with X(0)=X(L)=0.

Nontrivial solutions X_n = sin(nπx/L) occur only for λ_n = (nπ/L)², and T_n(t) = e^{−α λ_n t}. Each mode decays; higher modes decay faster.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Separation of variables relies on LINEARITY and homogeneous boundary conditions to superpose modes. Nonlinear PDEs generally can't be separated this way.

📊 FIGURE — The heat equation smooths everything out
Snapshots of a temperature profile: the jagged start (red) loses its sharp wiggles almost immediately (amber) and relaxes toward flat (green). Mathematically, mode n decays like e^(−k(nπ/L)²t) — the n² makes fine detail vanish fastest. Waves, by contrast, would keep ringing.
📊 FIGURE — separation of variables
🎯 EXAM TIP
Separation of variables assumes u(x, t) = X(x)·T(t) — a product of single-variable functions, never a sum. Substituting it and rearranging puts every x on one side and every t on the other; since the two sides depend on different variables they must both equal a constant, which turns the PDE into two ODEs.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Separation gives infinitely many product solutions (modes); Fourier series combine them to match ANY initial condition. Representing a function as a sum of sines and cosines is the engine of heat, wave, and signal analysis.

Fourier series
On [−L, L], f(x) = a₀/2 + Σ [aₙ cos(nπx/L) + bₙ sin(nπx/L)], with coefficients from integrals aₙ = (1/L)∫ f cos(nπx/L) dx, bₙ = (1/L)∫ f sin(nπx/L) dx. Sines/cosines are orthogonal, which isolates each coefficient.
WORKED EXAMPLE — matching an initial profile

A heat problem's solution is u(x,t) = Σ bₙ sin(nπx/L) e^{−αλₙt}. At t = 0 this must equal the initial profile f(x).

So the bₙ are exactly the Fourier sine coefficients of f(x) — computed by the integral formula. The series then evolves each mode in time.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Fourier coefficients are found by ORTHOGONALITY: integrating f against each basis function isolates one coefficient because the cross terms integrate to zero. This only works because sines/cosines are orthogonal.

📊 FIGURE — Fourier series building a square wave
One sine (indigo) is a blurry first draft of the square wave (dashed). Adding the 3rd harmonic (green) sharpens the corners; more terms keep flattening the tops and steepening the jumps. The persistent little overshoot at each jump is the Gibbs phenomenon.
"},"PDE/ch2/s3":{"body":"
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Putting it together: separation + Fourier series yields explicit series solutions of the heat and wave equations, and reveals their utterly different physics — one smooths, the other oscillates forever.

Heat vs wave solutions
Heat: u = Σ bₙ sin(nπx/L) e^{−αλₙt} — each mode DECAYS exponentially, so the solution smooths toward equilibrium. Wave: u = Σ sin(nπx/L)[Aₙcos(cλ√t...) ] oscillates — modes persist and vibrate, energy conserved.
WORKED EXAMPLE — heat vs wave behavior

Heat equation: the e^{−αλₙt} factors kill high-frequency modes fastest, so a jagged initial profile rapidly smooths to a gentle curve, then to zero.

Wave equation: modes carry cos/sin(ωₙt) factors — they oscillate forever (no decay), so a plucked string keeps vibrating; the shape recurs rather than smoothing.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The heat equation is IRREVERSIBLE (information smooths away — you can't run it backward stably); the wave equation is REVERSIBLE and oscillatory. Same solution method, opposite physics.

📊 FIGURE — The heat equation smooths everything out
Snapshots of a temperature profile: the jagged start (red) loses its sharp wiggles almost immediately (amber) and relaxes toward flat (green). Mathematically, mode n decays like e^(−k(nπ/L)²t) — the n² makes fine detail vanish fastest. Waves, by contrast, would keep ringing.

Formulas & method

For a linear 2nd-order PDE A u_xx + B u_xy + C u_yy + ... = 0, the discriminant is D = B² − 4AC. Classify by sign: D > 0 hyperbolic, D = 0 parabolic, D < 0 elliptic.

Separation of variables. For u_t = k u_xx on 0 ≤ x ≤ L with u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0, writing u = X(x)T(t) gives X'' + λX = 0 with X(0)=X(L)=0. The eigenvalues are

λ_n = (nπ / L)²,   n = 1, 2, 3, ...

with eigenfunctions X_n = sin(nπx/L).

Fourier sine coefficient

To expand f(x) on [0,L] in sines, b_n = (2/L) ∫₀ᴸ f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx. Example: f(x)=1 on [0,π] gives b_n = (2/π)∫₀^π sin(nx)dx = (2/nπ)(1 − (−1)ⁿ), so b_1 = 4/π.

Heat solution term

Each mode evolves as u_n(x,t) = b_n sin(nπx/L) e^{−(nπ/L)² k t}. Evaluate at a point by substituting x and t; recall sin(π/2)=1.

Formulas & method

Fourier series on [−π,π]: f(x) = a₀/2 + Σ (aₙ cos nx + bₙ sin nx) with

a₀ = (1/π) ∫₋π^π f dx\naₙ = (1/π) ∫₋π^π f cos(nx) dx\nbₙ = (1/π) ∫₋π^π f sin(nx) dx

Odd f gives all aₙ = 0; even f gives all bₙ = 0. Useful results: for f(x)=x², aₙ = 4(−1)ⁿ/n²; for f(x)=x, bₙ = 2(−1)^{n+1}/n.

d'Alembert (wave equation)

For u_tt = c² u_xx with u(x,0)=f(x), u_t(x,0)=g(x):

u(x,t) = ½[f(x+ct) + f(x−ct)] + (1/2c) ∫_{x−ct}^{x+ct} g(s) ds

Verifying a solution

Compute the needed derivatives and match: u_t = u_xx is heat; u_tt = u_xx is wave; u_xx + u_yy = 0 is Laplace.

Steady state (1-D Laplace)

u_xx = 0 gives a linear profile u(x) = u(0) + [u(L)−u(0)] x/L.

Formulas & method

For a linear second-order PDE written as A·u_xx + B·u_xy + C·u_yy + ... = 0, the character is fixed by the discriminant D = B² − 4AC:

  • Hyperbolic when D is positive (wave-like).
  • Parabolic when D equals 0 (heat-like).
  • Elliptic when D is negative (Laplace-like).

Separation eigenvalues. Solving X'' + λX = 0 on the interval [0, L] with X(0) = X(L) = 0 forces the eigenvalues λ_n = (nπ/L)² for n = 1, 2, 3, … with eigenfunctions sin(nπx/L).

Fourier sine coefficients

To expand f(x) on [0, L] in sines, use b_n = (2/L) ∫₀^L f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx. For the constant f(x) = 1 this gives b_n = (2/(nπ))(1 − (−1)ⁿ), which is 4/(nπ) for odd n and 0 for even n.

Heat-equation term

Each mode of u_t = k·u_xx on [0, L] has the form u_n(x,t) = b_n · sin(nπx/L) · e^(−(nπ/L)²·k·t). At t = 0 the exponential is 1, so the term reduces to b_n · sin(nπx/L).

Mini-example. For u_xx + 4u_xy + u_yy = 0, D = 4² − 4(1)(1) = 12, positive, so the PDE is hyperbolic.

"},"PDE/solving2/sv2":{"body":"

Formulas & method

Fourier coefficients on [−L, L]. With a_0 = (1/L) ∫₋L^L f(x) dx and a_n = (1/L) ∫₋L^L f(x) cos(nπx/L) dx. An odd f (like x) integrates to 0 against 1 and against cosines; an even f (like x²) can give nonzero values.

d'Alembert wave solution

For u_tt = c²·u_xx with u(x,0) = f(x) and u_t(x,0) = g(x):

u(x,t) = ½[f(x−ct) + f(x+ct)] + (1/2c) ∫(x−ct)^(x+ct) g(s) ds

If g = 0 only the average of f remains; if f = 0 only the integral term remains.

Identifying a PDE

Differentiate the candidate function and match: u_t = k·u_xx is the heat equation, u_tt = c²·u_xx is the wave equation, and u_xx + u_yy = 0 is Laplace's equation.

Steady-state (Laplace) in 1D

Steady state means u_xx = 0, so u is linear: u(x) = u(0) + [(u(L) − u(0))/L]·x.

Mini-example. With u(0) = 0, u(2) = 8, the steady state is u(x) = 4x, so u(1) = 4.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

\n
THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
\n
THE 3-STEP LOOP
\n\n\n\n
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
\n
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
\n\n\n\n\n
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.

23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
\nStart the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
\n
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
\n
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
\n
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers \"learn it in 25 minutes\" instead of hours.
